doc.title: "Papa Jack" Laine, Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine and Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1959-02-27

title: Kindergarten band in Biloxi and the lost spirit of Mardi Gras bands
summary: Around 1910 Laine's band of kids in Biloxi plays Kentucky Days and wins over a soldier band; he then says ragtime bands beat stiff military bands in parades and he ran up to five bands.

bands.name: Mississippi Hook and Ladder military band

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: I was over, this was around about 1910. Somewhere along around 1910. I was in Biloxi. I had three bands in Biloxi. I had a junior band playing for the junior company. I had one for the West End and one for a volunteer. Three bands. Well, I had all kids. All youngsters ranged in Biloxi, I guess they'd say, from about 16 years down to eight. I had 14 pieces in that band. Mississippi Hook and Ladder was right across the park where we were in, what's the name, Kennedy's Hotel. The park was like here, Kennedy's Hotel there. Mississippi Hook and Ladder was over here, right alongside the park. They had a military band. They played some kind of a tour. I remember that I heard of it. But anyhow, they were running, all the kids, you know, all my bunch of kids was running around Biloxi all that morning. They were all in uniform too. And these soldiers kept us saying that kindergarten band, the kindergarten band, you understand? They were all in uniform. So, all right, we were about to leave to go and meet the parade. The soldier band stood in the middle of the park and they played this piece. I remember now, I knew it. I knew what piece it was. And I got, I lined it up, all the kids, right before Kennedy's Hotel. I made them play Kentucky Days. The gentleman, I swear before Christ, they all took their hats off. All them soldiers took their hats off, you know, and clapped, and clapped, and clapped. They found out there was no kindergarten band. Them kids played music. Oh, Jesus, they played music, you know. And Haley Brunus, and Georgie Brunus, and Merit Brunus, and Abby Brunus, and had Kaz Out. Oh, yeah, Jones Kaz Out. All them kids, you know, brothers, they played music. And I stood right between them and told them how to come down. You played, you played piano, you know. You played mostly ragtime style, didn't you? All ragtime music. All ragtime. All ragtime music. Outside of Maltese, Johnny, in Maltese. Yeah. Outside of Maltese and Maltese, everything was right. They've sort of gotten away from that nowadays. I think the bands, they shouldn't have ragtime bands or jazz bands in the Mardi Gras parades. Instead of these stiff military bands. Yeah. They ought to have that, the spirit. That's right. The spirit is not there from the military march. That's right. No. They've lost that. When we'd be in the Mardi Gras parades, Johnny, three and four bands, you could hear them clapping all along the road. Every time they'd hear our bands play. They used to have Bowler, Red Bowler, Big Red Bowler, he's a military band used to play too. I know him. He used to play military bands. Oh, they used to play that stretch. Yeah. See? And we'd rag it. They'd go for that, like nobody's business. They always did. All they did. Go for that, like nobody's business. Yeah. More music in it. The other is too stiff sounding. That's it. That's it. I can remember. Gentlemen. Well, I couldn't feel the engagements, I'll tell you the Christ's truth. And I had five bands going. I couldn't feel the engagements. I've seen them put off parties and picnics at Millenburg. Till I was able to furnish them a contract. Those were wonderful days, you know. They used to be a lot of people. They used to be a lot of people. They used to be a lot of people. They used to be a lot of people. They used to be a lot of people.
